title: Puglia's Methane Premium Keeps Widening Even As Italy Tries to Catch Up
dek: Benzina and Gasolio in Puglia both nudged up half a percent overnight, but the real story is eight weeks of Metano climbing faster locally than nationally — and GPL doing the opposite.
executive_summary: As of September 12, self-service Benzina in Puglia sits at €2.1159 a litre and Gasolio at €2.2294, both up roughly half a percent from the day before and both essentially level with the national self-service averages of €2.1117 and €2.2361 respectively. GPL is the region's standout bargain at €0.7053 against a national €0.7543 — a gap of nearly 6.5% — while Metano is the mirror image, at €1.849 against Italy's €1.7256, over 7% above the national mark. Puglia's 1,579 registered stations, 1,434 of them (90.8%) reporting prices today, track close to the national reporting rate of 90.2%.

Zoom out to the eight weeks of data behind today's snapshot and a sharper pattern emerges: Metano has risen nationally by 13.2% since the week of July 20, actually outpacing Puglia's own 8.5% rise over the same stretch — Italy's methane prices are converging upward toward Puglia's level rather than the other way around, and the regional premium has narrowed from about 11.6% to roughly 7% even as both keep climbing. GPL tells the opposite story: Puglia's price has drifted down 1.4% since late July while the national average has barely moved, a modest but persistent divergence that's made the region's GPL premium over rivals even more pronounced than it was two months ago.

fuel_sections.heading: Benzina Tracks the National Line, Almost to the Cent
paragraphs: Self-service Benzina in Puglia closed at €2.1159 per litre on September 12, up €0.0102 (+0.48%) from €2.1057 the day before. That puts the region just €0.0042 above the national self-service average of €2.1117 — a gap of only 0.2%, tight enough that Puglia is effectively pricing in line with the rest of the country rather than standing out in either direction.

The eight-week trend backs that up: Puglia's weekly Benzina average rose from €1.9839 in the week of July 20 to €2.0962 in the week of September 7, a 5.66% increase, versus a near-identical 5.58% nationally (from €1.9756 to €2.0858). Both series show the same shape — a flattish plateau through early-to-mid August, then a steady climb from late August onward — which suggests Puglia's pump prices are being driven by the same national cost pressures as everywhere else, not by anything regional.

fuel_sections.heading: Diesel's Slow Comeback Runs a Touch Hotter in Puglia
paragraphs: Gasolio self-service in Puglia reached €2.2294 on September 12, up €0.0107 (+0.48%) day over day, landing €0.0067 below the national self-service average of €2.2361 — a modest 0.3% discount versus the rest of Italy.

The weekly series shows diesel actually falling through most of August before turning around: Puglia's average dropped from €2.1672 (week of July 20) to a low of €2.1159 (week of August 10), then climbed back to €2.2094 by the week of September 7 — a 4.42% rise off that bottom. Nationally the same low-then-recover pattern played out, from €2.1133 up to €2.2115, a slightly larger 4.65% rebound. Over the full eight weeks Puglia is up 1.95% against a national 1.69% gain, so the region's diesel has run marginally hotter than the country as a whole through this recovery, even though today's price still sits a hair under the national figure.

fuel_sections.heading: GPL Stays Puglia's Cheapest Fuel, and It's Getting Cheaper Still
paragraphs: GPL self-service held flat in Puglia at €0.7053 on September 12, unchanged from the day before. The bigger number is the gap to the rest of Italy: at a national self-service average of €0.7543, Puglia is pricing GPL €0.0490 lower — a 6.5% discount that makes it by far the region's cheapest fuel relative to its national counterpart.

That discount has been widening, not shrinking. Puglia's weekly GPL average slipped from €0.7148 in the week of July 20 to €0.7047 by the week of September 7, a 1.41% decline, while the national average barely moved over the same period, dropping just 0.54% (from €0.7592 to €0.7551). Eight straight weeks of gentle regional softening against a nearly flat national line means Puglia's GPL edge over the rest of the country has only grown since midsummer.

fuel_sections.heading: Metano's Steepest Climb Yet, But Italy Is Closing the Gap
paragraphs: Metano self-service in Puglia held at €1.849 on September 12, flat versus the previous day, but still the region's most expensive fuel relative to the rest of Italy: at €1.7256 nationally, Puglia sits €0.1234 above the national self-service average, a 7.15% premium.

The multi-week trend is the most dramatic of any fuel this period. Puglia's weekly Metano average climbed from €1.674 (week of July 20) to €1.8157 (week of September 7), an 8.47% rise — but that's actually outpaced by the national move, which jumped 13.15% over the same span, from €1.4999 to €1.6971. Both series were essentially flat through early-to-mid August before a sharp inflection in late August and September (Puglia's daily figure alone jumped from €1.649 to €1.849 between August 30 and September 11). The practical effect: Italy is closing in on Puglia's Metano price rather than the other way around, with the regional premium narrowing from roughly 11.6% in late July to about 7% today, even as both keep rising.

network_section.heading: Puglia's Station Network Is Reporting Right in Line With the National Average
paragraphs: Puglia has 1,579 registered fuel stations as of today's data pull, of which 1,434 reported at least one price — a 90.8% reporting rate. That's essentially identical to Italy's national reporting rate of 90.2% (21,649 of 23,999 registered stations), so the region isn't an outlier in either direction on data completeness: whatever price movements show up in today's Puglia figures reflect the same breadth of coverage you'd see nationally, not a thinner or noisier sample.

The registered count has stayed remarkably stable across the eight weeks of history behind this report, hovering between 1,575 and 1,579 stations, with daily reporting counts fluctuating in a tight band around 1,430-1,436. That stability is itself informative: it means the price trends described above are being measured against a consistent, near-constant panel of stations rather than a shifting one, so week-over-week changes in the average price reflect actual price movement rather than which stations happened to report that day.

methodology_section.heading: How This Report Gets Made — Automatically, Every Day
paragraphs: Everything above — the daily price pull from Italy's MIMIT open-data feed, the join against the national station registry, the region-of-the-day rotation that picked Puglia today, the week-by-week trend analysis, and the prose you're reading right now — is produced by an unattended pipeline built with Claude Code. A scheduled agent downloads or ingests the day's CSVs, recomputes the national and regional datasets, deterministically selects a region using a date-based rotation (so every one of Italy's 20 regions gets equal, predictable coverage over a 20-day cycle), and then writes and lays out this report from the resulting numbers, all without a human touching a spreadsheet.

That stands in contrast to how a report like this would traditionally get built: someone manually downloading a CSV each morning, pasting it into Excel, recalculating averages and week-over-week deltas by hand, and writing up the findings before anyone can read them. The manual version doesn't scale past one or two regions and tends to slip when the person maintaining it is busy or on leave. The automated version costs the same effort whether it covers one region or all twenty, runs on the same schedule every day, and — as this section demonstrates — can also explain its own trends without a human drafting the write-up first.

closing.heading: Every Region Gets Its Turn
paragraphs: Puglia is today's spotlight, but the same daily figures — Benzina, Gasolio, GPL, and Metano, self-service and served, down to the provincia and comune level — are live for all 20 Italian regions on the Fuel Dashboard at https://adeo-blip.github.io/fuel-price-italy/. Filter to your own region or provincia, compare it against the national trend, and check back tomorrow for whichever region comes up next in the rotation.

pull_quote: Since late July, Italy's national Metano price has climbed 13.2% — faster than Puglia's own 8.5% rise — closing a regional gap that started at 11.6% down to about 7% today.
caption:
Today's Fuel Dashboard spotlight is on Puglia, and the most interesting number isn't the daily price — it's the trend underneath it. Over the past eight weeks, Italy's national Metano price has actually risen faster (+13.2%) than Puglia's own already-elevated price (+8.5%), meaning the rest of the country is catching up to what Puglia has been paying at the pump for methane. Meanwhile Puglia's GPL, already the region's cheapest fuel by a wide margin, has kept drifting down relative to the national average — a 6.5% discount that's still widening.

Fuel Dashboard tracks Benzina, Gasolio, GPL, and Metano prices across all 20 Italian regions, every provincia, and thousands of comuni, refreshed daily from Italy's official MIMIT open-data feed. You can explore it live at https://adeo-blip.github.io/fuel-price-italy/.

What I think is worth calling out: this entire dashboard, the daily data pipeline, the region-of-the-day report, and even the analysis paragraphs above were built and are run end-to-end with Claude Code — no manually-maintained Excel sheet, no person recalculating weekly averages by hand. It updates itself every morning. That's the case for using AI coding tools for this kind of ongoing data project: the marginal cost of covering one more region, one more fuel, or one more day is close to zero once the pipeline exists, which just isn't true of a spreadsheet someone has to babysit.
